primary_claim: Gradient descent on token input embeddings (before positional encoding) reliably converges to near-zero loss while embeddings travel only a short distance and land back-projected in essentially the same token, consistent with the hypothesis that the input-embedding optimization landscape is overparameterized with a global-minima manifold that is 'close to everywhere'.

effect.metric: KL-divergence convergence and L2 distance traveled by input embeddings
effect.value: mean KL divergence approaches ~0 (under 1e-2 within <1,000 iterations for both models); embedding L2 movement stays small relative to typical inter-token distance (e.g. ~0.8 traveled vs ~2.5 max distance for the 'bark'/'neigh' example); cosine similarity of movement toward the target token only ~0.3

stated_future_work: This is the first in a planned series of posts investigating whether meaningful information or interesting behavior can be extracted from gradients on input embedding space
limitations_stated: Hand-rolling a custom ADAM optimizer for the Llama experiment was a mistake and caused avoidable issues
No effort was initially put into optimization, making a batch of 64 take ~11 seconds per step on a MacBook Air
The 'bark' example is a contrived outlier compared to the broader 64-example set
The reason random input embeddings' back-projections changed (unlike ModernBERT's) despite similarly small movement is unclear
quote: The evidence we collected seems to support the hypothesis that the global loss minima manifold for `Meta-LLama/Llama-3.2-1B` is "close to everywhere" and easy to find through gradient descent.
